title: Imposing Hard Constraints on Deep Networks: Promises and Limitations
authors: Pablo Marquez-Neila, Mathieu Salzmann, Pascal Fua
venue: CVPR 2017 Workshop on Negative Results in Computer Vision (arXiv:1706.02025)
conclusions: Formulates hard-constraint DNN training as KKT/Lagrangian systems solved with Krylov subspace methods (MINRES-QLP) to handle million-parameter networks, since directly forming/inverting the KKT matrix is infeasible at that scale.
Shows hard-constraint training (Hard-SGD, Hard-Adam) is computationally tractable and gives 'reasonable' results, refuting the belief that it is intractable for deep nets.

But empirically, on 3D human-pose estimation (Human3.6M) with symmetry constraints, hard constraints do NOT outperform soft penalty constraints (Soft-Adam is best, Hard-SGD close behind); hard methods are also 10-100x slower.

Hard-constraint methods do not guarantee perfect constraint satisfaction in practice (not even on training data) because only a random subset of constraints is enforced (linearized) at each iteration, so previously-satisfied constraints can become violated again.

A synthetic hypersphere experiment reproduces the same qualitative failure: with mildly incompatible/near-linear-dependent constraints, hard (KKT) updates behave erratically while soft penalties converge more smoothly to a comparable solution.
Conclusion: hard constraints on deep nets are practical but, in this study, offer no advantage over soft penalties; the paper is explicitly framed as a negative result.
